batch.title: Direction audit — corrections + unclear units (23 Oct 2026)
batch.notes: Every effect unit was re-coded blind; disagreements were adjudicated against the quote. Corrections are listed first (approve if right), then units whose direction the quote cannot settle. The claim line now reads the direction in plain words (e.g. '↓ less erosion · benefit of the practice').

units.citation: Castle, S. E. et al. (2021). The impacts of agroforestry on agricultural productivity, ecosystem services, and human well‐being in low‐ and middle‐income countries: A systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews.
units.quote: The average effect of these interventions on household income outcomes is 0.12 standardized mean difference (Hedges' g) with a 95% CI of [−0.06, 0.30] (p = .20), which we calculated under a random effects model. This result indicates that there is an overall small, positive, but statistically insignificant, effect of agroforestry interventions on incomes. In aggregate, then, studied agroforestry interventions have improved incomes either through improved yields or through PES or higher prices received by eco-certification.

relationship.outcome_raw: income improvement pathways aggregate conclusion

units.quote:
Hydrological features defined for these
analyses (Table 1) appeared to be recovered immediately after
restoration (Figure 1A), but see Cole [18], Hunt et al. [19], Ahn
and Dee [20], and Kumar and Zhao [21] for deeper consider-
ations of challenges to hydrologic restoration in wetlands (from
factors like climate variation [20] or complex flow paths of water
through heterogeneous vegetation and soils [21]). In addition, all

units.citation: Muthuri et al. (2023). Agroforestry's contribution to livelihoods and carbon sequestration in East Africa: A systematic review. Trees, Forests and People.
units.quote: This review shows that agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 ± 12.2 Mg C ha−1 in the soil (Fig. 3). The combined estimate of carbon in biomass and the soil is larger than what was estimated to be the potential carbon storage (29–53 Mg C ha−1) of agrosilvicultural systems in the humid tropics of Africa (Albrecht and Kandji, 2003), but lower than systems with high stem density, large mean tree size, and longer maximum ages i.e. over 60 years reported in Southeast Asia (Roshetko et al., 2007). The difference with earlier estimates is mostly in the soil part where several method­ ological issues need to be considered (Hairiah et al., 2020), such as variation in the soil depth included and changes in soil bulk density that influence which soil is included in a fixed-depth sample (Schrumpf et al., 2011). The amount varies depending on agroforestry practice, ranging from 26.7 ± 7.0 Mg C ha−1 in improved fallows to 153±23 Mg C ha−1 in homegardens.

relationship.outcome_raw: agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 98.8 +/- 12.2 Mg C per ha in the soil

context.note: Pooled mean +/- SE (12.2). Soil holds ~4x the biomass pool. Systematic review of 185 East-African publications (livelihoods n = 152, carbon n = 43). NOTE: these are carbon STOCKS (Mg C per ha), not sequestration RATES — a rate requires a time denominator the review does not give.

units.citation: Reed et al. (2017). Trees for life: The ecosystem service contribution of trees to food production and livelihoods in the tropics. Forest Policy and Economics.
units.quote: The overall trend across the studies shows that in the majority of cases (52%) there was a net positive (47%) or neutral (5%) effect of tree presence on food yields or food yield proxies. However, when the results are disaggregated by region, there is a degree of variability (Fig. 5). For example, in the Americas and Asia, tree presence was more likely to enhance food yields with positive effects of trees on yields reported in 58% and 54% of studies for these regions respectively; while in Asia the opposite is the case, with the majority of studies (48%) reporting decreased food yields as a result of tree presence (Fig. 5).

relationship.outcome_raw: in the majority of cases (52%) tree presence had a net positive (47%) or neutral (5%) effect on food yields or yield proxies; regionally, positive effects were reported in 58% (Americas) and 54% (Asia) of studies while a further statement reports 48% of studies in one region recording DECREASED yields

context.note: HEADLINE. QUEUE/SOURCE CAVEAT: the regional sentence names 'Asia' twice with opposite signs — an apparent typo in the published text (the 48%-decrease region is almost certainly Africa per the later regional breakdown 33%/48%/33%). Not resolvable from the text, so no regional unit emitted from this sentence. VOTE-COUNT review: percentages are shares of STUDIES reporting a direction, not effect magnitudes, so metric = narrative. PICOS: 58 of the 74 reviewed studies are agroforestry studies and 53 of those are trees INTRODUCED TO THE FARM (typically alley cropping); only 12 studies concern off-farm natural forest patches. The pooled vote-counts are therefore dominated by, but not exclusive to, agroforestry — read as agroforestry-weighted, not agroforestry-pure.

units.citation: Reed et al. (2017). Trees for life: The ecosystem service contribution of trees to food production and livelihoods in the tropics. Forest Policy and Economics.
units.quote: The main difference when comparing the effects of trees on yields with the overall livelihood effects of trees across all studies is the reduc- tion in the total negative effects from 36% for yield to 16% for overall livelihood effects, suggesting that a reduction in yields may be compen- sated by other beneﬁts provided by trees to the farm system (Fig. 6). This cost/beneﬁt relationship—where the cost of crop yield losses is compensated by the overall beneﬁts of incorporating trees—is consis- tent across the study regions with Africa, Asia and the Americas reporting negative effects of trees on crop yields in 33%, 48%, and 33% of studies but negative effects of trees on overall livelihood outcomes in only 15%, 24%, and 8% respectively (Fig. 7).

units.quote: a barragem subterrânea não constitui a principal fonte de renda da família da área em estudo;  devido a intempéries climáticas, não se colheu nada na barragem subterrânea no ano agrícola 2005/2006 (Tabela 6.5);  terceirização de mão-de-obra, pelo fato de os filhos, ao atingirem certa idade, foram estudar na cidade. Como pontos relevantes, foram identificados:  valorização da terra (conservação do solo); diversificação agríco- la; melhoria na qualidade do solo (fertilidade do solo);  aumento da renda familiar e melhoria na qualidade de vida da família (impacto social e econômico). As produtividades alcançadas (Tabela 6.5) demonstram que a barra- gem subterrânea constitui-se em uma alternativa tecnológica que pro- porciona garantia ao agricultor de obter sua safra, desde que se tenha o mínimo de chuva necessário (Tabela 6.6) para atender às necessida- des das culturas exploradas. (English: the subsurface dam is not the main source of income of the family in the area studied; due to climatic adversities, nothing was harvested from the subsurface dam in the 2005/2006 agricultural year (Table 6.5); outsourcing of labour, because the children, on reaching a certain age, went to study in the city. As relevant points the following were identified: valuation of the land (soil conservation); agricultural diversification; improvement of soil quality (soil fertility); increase in family income and improvement in the family's quality of life (social and economic impact). The yields achieved (Table 6.5) show that the subsurface dam is a technological alternative that gives the farmer a guarantee of obtaining a harvest, provided the minimum rainfall needed (Table 6.6) to meet the needs of the crops grown occurs.)

units.quote:
Sedge communities on the peatland Dokudovskoe (1,200 ha) occupy no more 
than 20 ha 
End of Project Target  
Sedge communities on peatland Dokudovskoe occupy at least 700 ha 
End of Project Status 
By 2020, pilot activities on creation of sedge communities underway on 950 
hectares of cultivated peat bog. Dokudovskoe  peatland rewetted (950 ha). 
Activities for accelerated restoration of open sedge marshes were planned 
for an area of about 700 ha in 2021, using machinery for soil preparation, 
collection and sowing of seeds of marsh plants. However, for three years in 
the natural bogs of Sporoske and Zvanets sedge seeds were practically absent 
for unknown reasons. Therefore, marsh plants were planted and a small 
amount of sedge seeds were used on an area of 70 ha.  
On the rest of the area prepared for planting of marsh plants seeds, 
restoration took place naturally. In this regard, reed and cattail were the first 
to appear on these areas, which in the process of development will be 
replaced by sedge communities  
Mapping of vegetation in the Dokudovskoe  peatland conducted in July-
August 2021; 2021-2022 monitoring activities determined the area of 
reinstated bog plant communities: Phragmites-sedge communities (Carex 
acuta, C. rostrata, C. pseudocyperus, Phragmites australis) on peatland 
Dokudovskoe occupy at least 398 ha (botanical report).

units.quote:
Conversely, all restored wetlands had a net warm-
ing effect (figure 5b), because of their relatively young age
and the impossibility for CH4 emissions to equilibrate in
the atmosphere. This suggests that restored wetlands do
not directly mitigate radiative warming at the yearly to dec-
adal time-scale, even though they can accumulate carbon in
their soil.

relationship.outcome_raw: NET radiative balance of carbon dioxide uptake and methane emission of restored and rewetted wetlands, counted from the restoration year: net WARMING at the yearly to decadal timescale because the wetlands are young and methane has not equilibrated; the drained-state carbon dioxide emissions that rewetting stops are NOT netted in

units.citation: BADOLA et al. (2005). Valuing ecosystem functions: an empirical study on the storm protection function of Bhitarkanika mangrove ecosystem, India. Environmental Conservation.
units.quote:
The greatest
damage to ﬁsh seedlings per household (LFS) was in Singdi,
where INR 310.8 ± 144.97 (US$ 6.91) of seedlings released
were washed away, and the least damage was in Bankual (INR
69.7 ± 32.20, US$ 1.55; Table 3).

relationship.outcome_raw: loss of fish fingerlings washed out of ponds per household: lowest in the mangrove village but the difference is not significant

context.practice_as_described: No intervention: the EXISTING Bhitarkanika mangrove forest. 'a village in the shadow of mangrove' (Bankual, 0 km from the forest) compared with 'a village not in the shadow of mangrove and having no embankment' (Singdi, 9.2 km) and 'a village not in the shadow of mangrove, but with an embankment on the seaward side' (Bandhamal); the three villages chosen equidistant from the sea
context.note: damage-cost-avoided study after the October 1999 Orissa super cyclone (p3: 'in the wake of this super cyclone'); 100% door-to-door survey of the three villages; one-way ANOVA across the THREE villages (Table 4), no pairwise mangrove-vs-unprotected test reported, so significance is left not_reported unless the text says otherwise; the comparison used here is mangrove-sheltered Bankual vs unprotected Singdi; the embankment village (Bandhamal) is a grey-infrastructure arm, not the counterfactual. Authors call the evidence 'only indicative' and 'not conclusive' (p6). Table 4 LFS p=0.227 (ns), so encoded as a null despite the point estimates in the quote.

units.question: Direction unclear — Quote shows less damage in mangrove village; significance not in quote. Approve = keep as coded; reject with a reason if wrong.

plain.direction_reads: ○ no clear effect
plain.practice: Practice: mangrove restoration → tidal coastal (Mangrove restoration; Ecological mangrove restoration (EMR)).
plain.described: The source describes what was done as: “No intervention: the EXISTING Bhitarkanika mangrove forest. 'a village in the shadow of mangrove' (Bankual, 0 km from the forest) compared with 'a village not in the shadow of mangrove and having no embankment' (Singdi, 9.2 km) and 'a village not in the shadow of mangrove, but with an embankment on the seaward side' (Bandhamal); the three villages chosen equidistant from the sea”.
